questions.q: Why should you rule out your own setup before concluding a paper's result doesn't reproduce?
options: The base rate for the problem being in your own setup, rather than the paper, is high
It's a legal requirement before contacting authors
Papers are never wrong
Your setup is irrelevant to the outcome
questions.explain: Most reproduction mismatches trace back to the reproducer's own environment, code version, or settings rather than a genuine flaw in the original result, so ruling that out first is the efficient first step.

questions.q: What is 'dependency drift' and why does it matter for reproduction attempts?
options: A change in a paper's abstract over multiple arXiv versions
Changes in library, CUDA, or language versions between a paper's release and your own run, which can silently change behavior
A researcher switching institutions mid-project
A dataset being renamed
questions.explain: Code written against older library or CUDA versions can behave differently when run with newer dependencies, which is a common and easily overlooked cause of a reproduction mismatch.

questions.q: Before emailing the original authors, what should you check first?
options: Nothing — email them immediately
The paper's repository issues and forks, since the mismatch may already be reported with a fix or explanation
Whether the paper has been cited more than 100 times
Whether the authors are still affiliated with the same institution
questions.explain: Checking existing issues and forks first can surface a known caveat or fix without needing to contact the authors at all.

questions.q: What distinguishes a good email to paper authors about a reproducibility issue from a poor one?
options: A good email is as long as possible
A good email states exactly what was run, what was expected, what was ruled out, and asks one specific question
A good email avoids mentioning what you've already tried
A good email should be sent to as many co-authors as possible to increase the odds of a reply
questions.explain: Specific, well-documented questions get specific answers; vague reports like 'it doesn't work' tend to get vague or no replies.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what kind of claim is defensible after a thorough, documented reproduction failure?
options: "This paper is definitely fraudulent"
"I could not reproduce result X under conditions Y"
No claim should ever be made public
"This entire field of research is unreliable"
questions.explain: A precisely scoped claim about what was attempted and what happened is defensible and useful; a sweeping claim that the paper or field is wrong requires ruling out every alternative explanation first.
